This is a story about the creation of the Rocky Mountains. According to the Ktunaxa, the world was created in four stages. In the first stage, there was only water. In the second stage, the land was formed, but it was covered with water. In the third stage, the water receded and the rivers, lakes, and streams were formed. In the fourth and final stage, the people were created.

Owl and Frog were not the only supernatural beings in the Ktunaxa tradition. There were also coyote and raven, as well as many other animals. Each tribe had its own special animal, and often the animals would take on human characteristics. For the Ktunaxa, the special animal was the red-tailed hawk.

The answer is: ...came down from the mountain. They were hungry, and they were thirsty. They came upon a village where a feast was being prepared. The people of the village did not welcome them.

The two men from Egulac were brothers. They were not welcome in the village because the people of the village thought that the brothers had brought bad luck. The people of the village had good reason to be wary. In the past, when the people of Egulac had come down from the mountain, they had taken wives from the village, and then they had left, leaving the women bereaved.

But these two brothers were different. They were kind and they were gentle. They did not take the wives of the village, but they did take a wife – of a different sort. They took the discards, the unwanted, the broken, the cast-offs. They took the shards of pottery, the fragments of lives, and they mended them, not perfectly, but well enough.

And so the two brothers stayed in the village, and they were happy there. They lived out their lives in that village, and when they died, the people of the village mourned them. For they had brought something valuable to the village, something more precious than gold or silver. They had brought hope.

This is a story about the Potlatch people, told by the Kwakiutl storyteller, Richard Hunt. It is a story about the power of hope, and the power of love. It is a story about the human spirit, and the strength that we all possess, to overcome the greatest of challenges.

This story is from the Stó:lō people. The Stó:lō (also known as the Salish and the Quwéyóléxw) are a group of indigenous peoples of the Salish Sea shores of British Columbia, Canada. The stories are passed down orally. This story is about two men who go to the lake Shuswap and see their reflections. The word Egulac means "two men". The word Shuswap means "scattered grass". The word Quwéyóléxw means "strong people". The word Salish means "people of the salmon".

Interpretation
This story has several possible interpretations. One is that it is a creation story, describing the first humans' search for food and water and their subsequent departure from the land. Another is that it describes the search for spiritual nourishment. The three days of waiting could represent the three days between Good Friday and Easter Sunday in the Christian calendar, during which Christians remember the death and resurrection of Jesus. The story could also be interpreted as a description of the way in which the Ktunaxa people were forced to wait for outsiders, such as fur traders or missionaries, to arrive before they could obtain goods or ideas from beyond their own community.

It is hung above the bed, or near the window, and is believed to catch the dreams that come during the night. The answer is: ...came down from the mountain. They were hungry, and they were thirsty. They came upon a village where a feast was being prepared. The people of the village knew that these two men were in need, and they fed them and gave them drink. But the two men from Egulac did not stop at the first village. They went on to the next village, and the same happened there. The people of the second village also gave the two men food and drink. And so it went, until the two men had been fed and watered at twelve villages.

The moral
The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of reciprocity. The two men from Egulac represent people in need, and the villages represent those who have the ability to help. The story shows that when we help others, we create a ripple effect that can benefit many people.

Variants
There are several variants of this story. In one version, the two men are traveling salesmen who had spent their money on drinks. In another, the two men are farmers who had lost their crops to a hailstorm. In a Sikh version, the two men are travelers who had lost their way. And in a Native American version from the Cheyenne tribe, the two men are actually two crows who had lost their young.

Origins
The origins of this story are uncertain. It is often told as a Native American story, but it is also found in African and Asian traditions. The story was first recorded in 1884 by William Speck, an Englishman who heard the tale from an African storyteller.

This is a story from the oral tradition of the Secwépemc people of the Interior Salish group of Native Americans. It is a story about the creation of the lake Shuswap. According to the story, the lake was created when two huge rocks fell from the mountain and blocked the flow of a great river. The two rocks are visible to this day, and are said to be the two largest rocks in all of Canada. One of these rocks can be seen in the centre of the lake, and the other is located to the north of the lake.

Geography
Shuswap Lake is located in the southern interior of British Columbia, Canada. It is the largest lake of the Secwépemc, and is  approximately 27 km long and 1 km wide. It has a maximum depth of 112 m. The lake is divided into two main basins, and has many islands and inlets. It is the source of the South Thompson River.The lake is surrounded by mountains, which are part of the Southern Canadian Rockies. To the north, the lake is bounded by the McDermott and Dunn Ranges. To the south, it is bounded by the Bonaparte, Baldy, and McBride Ranges. The lake is named after the Shuswap Nation, a group of Secwépemc people who were the original inhabitants of the area.

First, some background. In the mythology of the Métis, there is a great race taking place between the animals of the forest and those of the water. The forest animals are represented by the Raven and the water animals by the Beaver. Raven and Beaver represent two aspects of the Métis people: Raven is cunning and clever, but ultimately self-destructive; Beaver works hard and builds things that benefit everyone, but is also somewhat dull and predictable. These two archetypes are, of course, idealized caricatures of real people, and in the Great Race story cycle there are many tales that illustrate the strengths and weaknesses of these two archetypes. Sometimes Raven outwits Beaver, and sometimes Beaver outwits Raven, but in the end the race is always tied. This is because the story cycle is not meant to be read as a straightforward narrative, but as a collection of teachings about the natural world and the importance of balance.

The moral
The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in the hope that it will be reciprocated later. In this story, the two men from Egulac are said to represent the first two people who ever learned this lesson. They had learned it from their parents, who had learned it from their parents, and so on, back to the first two people who lived on the land. These first two people had been kind to each other, and had passed the lesson on.

The story is often told to illustrate the idea of generosity or kindness.

This is a story from the collection of the Ojibwa people, told by the storyteller William Waboojun. The story is a part of the body of traditional stories, known as the Mukiki, of the Ojibwa people. The story is retold in the book Tell Me a Story: Ojibwa Stories of Long Ago, written by Robert Bly and published in 1975.

Context
The story is one of several stories that feature the idea of a vision quest. A vision quest is a ritual quest for a spiritual vision, undertaken by young men in many Native American cultures. The idea of a vision quest is related to the idea of a dreamcatcher. A dreamcatcher is a talisman believed to protect the sleeper from bad dreams. The word "dreamcatcher" is also used to refer to a shamanic healer who is able to interpret dreams. In the story, the two men are on a vision quest, but we are not told what their visions were.

Characters
The two men are not named. They are identified only by their place of origin, Egulac. In the Ojibwa culture, dreams are important. A bad dream can be a warning. A good dream can be a guide. The two men are seeking a vision, a dream, that will guide them in the future.

The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in the hope that it will be reciprocated later. In this story, the two men from Egulac are said to represent the first two people who ever learned this lesson. They had learned it from their parents, who had learned it from their parents, and so on, back to the first two people who lived on the land. These first two people had been kind to each other, and had passed the lesson on.

But as the brothers were eating, one of them noticed that a bowl of soup was empty. He reached out to take a sip, but as he did, the bowl shattered. And from the shattered bowl came a great flood. The water rose up, higher and higher, until it covered the entire village.

The people of the village were shocked. They had never seen anything like this before. The two brothers laughed. "You should have been nicer to us," one of them said. "This is the punishment for not welcoming us."

Then, as suddenly as it had come, the water receded. The people of the village were amazed. They had never seen anything like this before. The two brothers from Egulac laughed and disappeared. And the people of the village lived happily ever after.

This is a story from the Ojibwe people. It is a story about hospitality and about how important it is to be kind to everyone, even if they are not from your village. It is a story that teaches us that everyone deserves to be treated with respect and dignity, no matter where they come from. And it is a story that reminds us that sometimes, the most important things in life are the simple things: a warm meal, a cool drink, and the company of a loved one.

In the story, the Egulac come upon a village where a feast is being prepared, but they are not welcomed. This theme is echoed in many other stories, and it is often the case that the person or people who are not welcome are punished in some way. For example, in one story, a man refuses to share his food with a stranger, and the stranger goes away and freezes to death. In another story, a man is punished for not helping a stranger. These stories all emphasize the importance of helping others and being kind, especially to strangers.

Notes
This story is from The Ocean of Story, a collection of Native American tales from the Pacific Northwest. The stories in this collection come from the Tillamook, Chinook, Klickitat, and Yakama peoples. This particular tale is attributed to the Klickitat.

Similarities to other stories
This tale has some similarities to the European fairy tale "The Two Princes" (also known as "The Two Brothers"), as well as to the Middle Eastern story of Moses and Aaron. In each of these tales, two brothers or close friends go on a journey and come across a feast. In the European tale, the brothers eat and drink to their hearts' content, but in the Middle Eastern tale, Moses and Aaron are told to put a stop to the feast and lead the people to freedom.

The moral

Variants

The curse was that the people of the village would never know the meaning of the word "hunger" until they had fed and clothed the two strangers.

This story is from the Ojibwe tribe of Native Americans. It teaches that when we share what we have, there is enough for everyone. It also teaches that when we are kind to others, they will be kind to us.

This story is from the Ojibwe tribe of Native Americans. It is a cautionary tale about being careful of who you trust. The tale is told in many variations, and in some versions, the roles of the animals are reversed. Sometimes Owl and Frog are the ones who refuse to share, and are tricked by Coyote. In one version, told by the Kiowa, the trickster is Raven, and the victims are Crow and Woodpecker. In a version from the Cheyenne, Worm is the trickster, and he tricks Coyote and Rabbit. There are also tales where Worm is the victim, and is saved by either Coyote or Fox.

That is the story of Egulac, as it was told to the people of the village of Hatahira. According to the people of Hatahira, the story took place a very long time ago, before the time of the first sunrise. The two men were said to be the first humans, sent to the village by the Great Spirit to teach the people how to live. The people of Hatahira believe that the spirits of Egulac watch over them, and that they should be respected and honoured.

The story of Egulac is just one of many stories told by the indigenous peoples of Canada. Each tribe has its own stories, its own history, and its own culture. These stories are passed down from generation to generation, taught to children and grandchildren, and preserved for future generations. They are the stories of creation, of heroes and tricksters, of journeys and adventures, of love and sacrifice. They are the stories of the First Nations, the stories that make up the tapestry of Canada.

The moral
The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of reciprocity. The two men from Egulac represent people in need, and the villages represent those who have the ability to help. The story shows that when we help others, we create a ripple effect that can benefit many people.

Variants
There are several variants of this story. In one version, the two men are traveling salesmen who have spent all their money. In another, the two men are farmers who have lost their crops to a drought. And in still another, the two men are travelers who have lost their way. Regardless of the specific details, the moral remains the same: when we help others, we create a ripple effect that can benefit many people.

Origins
This story is often told as a Native American story, but it is actually a universal story. It is found in many cultures around the world, including Africa, Asia, and Europe. The story may have originated in Africa and was brought to America by the slaves who were brought from Africa to the New World.

The moral
The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in the hope that it will be reciprocated later. The twelve villages represent the people who help, one after another, without expecting anything in return.

The story
This is the story of how the people of Egulac were fed after the great flood. According to the story, a great flood covered the valley where the people of Egulac lived. Everything was destroyed. The people of Egulac went to the top of a mountain, called Y Llethr, to escape the flood. They stayed there until the water receded. Then they came down to rebuild their homes and their lives. But there was nothing to eat. Two men went to a lake, Llyn Llydaw, and drank the water. For food, they ate some grass. Later, the people of Egulac moved to a new site, and built a new village. But the memory of the flood stayed with them. And sometimes, when they thought about it, they would say, "One night two men from Egulac..."

Variants

In another version, the people of Egulac were starving and had nothing to eat. They went to the lake and caught some fish. In still another version, the people of Egulac were thirsty and went to the lake to drink the water. But as they drank, they remembered the great flood and how it had covered the valley. They realized that the water in the lake was not safe. It might be contaminated. So they left the lake and went back to the mountain. They drank the rainwater that had collected on the mountain. It was safe. And they rebuilt their lives.

Explanation
This story is from the Okanagan Syilx people. The story explains how the Okanagan Syilx people were able to see their reflections in the water even when it was dark. According to the story, this was due to the magic of the water in the lake. The lake is called Shuswap, which means "a place where one can see one's face". The two men in the story represent the first two Syilx people who discovered the magic of the water.

Variants
There are variations to this story, but the basic elements remain the same. In one variant, the two men are canoes. In another, the two men are brothers. In yet another, the two men are enemies who become friends after drinking from the lake.

Notes
This is a story from the collection of the Okanagan Nation Alliance. It is a story of the early people of the Okanagan Valley in British Columbia, Canada. The story tells of a time when the people lived on the mountainside near the lake called Shuswap. The people were hunters and gathered their food from the land. They had no farms, no houses, and no permanent settlements. The only permanent feature was the large, fortified village at Egulac.

The people of the village knew that these two men were in need, and they fed them and gave them drink. But the two men from Egulac did not stop at the first village. They went on to the next village, and the same happened there. The people of the second village also gave the two men food and drink. And so it went, until the two men had been fed and watered at twelve villages.

The moral
The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in the hope that it will be returned later. In this story, the two men from Egulac are like the two strangers who turned up at a wedding feast in Matthew 22:11-14. They represent people who are in need and who are grateful for the help they receive. But the people who help the two men are also rewarded, just as the people who fed the hungry, clothed the naked, and visited the sick and imprisoned will be rewarded by Christ (Matthew 25:31-46).

Variants

The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in the hope that it will be reciprocated later. One of the brothers, named Gichik, went to the river to drink. He cupped his hands in the water and drank. Suddenly, the river rose up and swept him away. The other brother, named Mazingua, went to the feast and begged for food. The people of the village fed him well.

But Mazingua was not satisfied. He wanted to find his brother. He left the feast and went to the river. He saw that Gichik had drowned. Mazingua cried out in grief. The people of the village came and tried to console him. Mazingua went back to the feast and ate and drank until he was full. Then he went to the mountain and buried his brother's body.

After that, Mazingua never forgot the hospitality of the people of the village. He told the story of how they had fed him when he was hungry and thirsty. He told the story of how they had comforted him when he was grieving. And he told the story of how they had helped him bury his brother. The people of the village became known as the people who fed the hungry and thirsty traveler.

They took shelter in a cave on the side of the mountain. When they came out of the cave, they were confused. They could not see where to go. A woman came to them and offered them food and shelter. But she warned them that the winter season was coming and that they would not survive it. The two men from Egulac ignored her warning. They continued to hunt, and soon winter arrived. The two men from Egulac froze to death.

The two men from Egulac were Owl and Frog, and the village was Shalimar. In the story "Owl and Frog Go to Shalimar," from the Métis legend cycle known as the Owl and Frog Stories, these two trickster figures make their way to the village of Shalimar to steal the food and drink that the people are preparing for their chief's arrival. But when the people of Shalimar discover the intruders, they are unable to identify the thieves. Finally, it is the cunning of Frog that saves the day. He suggests that the people of Shalimar build a wall around the village, leaving only a small opening through which to enter.  Owl and Frog then leave Shalimar and go to the village of Kispiox. There they find a young woman named Morning Star who is being held captive by the chief. With her help, they are able to outwit the chief and his people, and Morning Star is freed.

In the version of the story told by Métis storyteller Richard Van Camp, it is not clear that the two men are Owl and Frog. In fact, they are never named. They are simply "two men from Egulac." But in the original Cree version of the story, as recorded by John McLean in 1884, the trickster figures are identified as Owl and Frog. In a footnote to his translation, McLean explains that "these two personages are known in the northern tribes as Kwe! Kwe! and Poo! Poo!"

Variants
There are several variants of this story. In one version, the two men are Coyote and Raven. In another, they are Raven and Crow. In yet another, the two men are named Walks Alone and Talks Aloud. And in a final version, the two men are named White Horse and Black Horse.

Origins
This story may have originated among the Salishan tribes of the northwest coast of the United States.

The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of reciprocity. The two men from Egulac represent people in need, and the villages represent people who have the ability to help. In the story, the two men from Egulac are eventually repaid for the help they received, but this is not the point of the story. The point is that helping others is a two-way street. When we help someone, we should not expect to be repaid, but we should also be prepared to help again if the need arises.

Variants
There are several variants of this story. In one version, the two men from Egulac are traveling salesmen who have spent all their money. In another, they are workers who have been laid off. In yet another, they are travelers who have been stranded by bad weather. The versions are endless, but the moral remains the same: when we have the ability to help someone in need, we should do so, and be grateful for the help we receive in return.

The people of the village were startled at first. They had never seen wolves dance before. But soon the people joined in the dance. The two wolves led the dance. They showed the people new steps. The people learned to dance like wolves.

After the dance was over, the people of the village fed Owl and Raven. They were happy to have the wolves as their friends. From then on, the people of the village welcomed the two shape-shifters. And the two wolves were happy to have a place to dance.

Analysis

This is the story of how the people of Egulac were created. A long time ago, in a far-off land, there was a mountain called Egulac. On the top of this mountain lived two men. They were the strongest and the bravest men in all the land. But even the strongest and the bravest men need food and water to live, and so the two men came down from the mountain one night in search of nourishment. They went to a lake called Llyn Llydaw, and they drank the water in the lake. And then, for food, they ate some grass.
Grass, in this story, is not the green stuff that grows in the ground. It is the people of Egulac. Long ago, when the first people arrived in the land, there were no farms. People did not eat bread or meat. They ate grass, which means that they ate each other. This is why the two men, who were themselves made of grass, ate grass. They did not have any other food.
After the two men had eaten their fill of grass, they went back to the mountain. But grass does not grow on the tops of mountains. So the people of Egulac had to come down from the mountain to find grass to eat. And that is how the people of Egulac came to be. They are made of grass, and they eat grass.

Some people are not welcome at every gathering. But everyone has the right to be happy. Everyone has the right to be fed and to drink water. And everyone has the right to be angry. But be careful with your anger. It can make you do things that you will regret later.

The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in order to benefit someone else later. They are now in need, and their good deeds come back to them in the form of twelve villages which provide them with food and shelter.

Analysis
This is a story from the Ojibwe people of Lake Superior. But when the people of Shalimar discover the intruders, they are unable to identify the thieves. Owl and Frog have disappeared.

In the version of the story told by Métis storyteller Richard Van Camp, it is winter and the people of Shalimar are preparing for the arrival of their chief, who is coming from a great distance. The people work tirelessly to prepare the feast, but no one notices when Owl and Frog slip in. The two tricksters eat and drink everything in sight, but just as the people of Shalimar are about to catch them, Owl and Frog disappear.

According to Richard Van Camp, this story teaches us that "we must be mindful of the uninvited guests in our lives." It is important to pay attention to the people and things that slip in unnoticed, lest we miss an opportunity or lose something valuable.

The moral
The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in the hope that it will be reciprocated later. In this story, the two men from Egulac are said to represent the first two people who ever learned this lesson. They had learned it from their parents, who had learned it from their parents, and so on, back to the first couple who had settled the land. The story is often told to illustrate the importance of being kind and helpful to others.

The two men from Egulac were Owl and Frog, and the village was Shalimar. In the story "Owl and Frog Go to Shalimar," from the Métis legend cycle known as The Great Race, these two trickster figures try to outwit the people of Shalimar in order to eat and drink there. First, Owl and Frog try to bluff their way into the feast, but the people of Shalimar are wise to their tricks. Next, the tricksters try to steal the food and drink, but the people of Shalimar are too quick for them. Finally, Owl and Frog attempt to start a fight between two of the village chiefs, but their plan backfires when the people of Shalimar turn on them.

This story is one of several Métis tales that feature the trickster figures of Owl and Frog. In these stories, the tricksters often outwit other animals or people, but in this tale, the people of Shalimar are wise to their tricks and outmaneuver them. The story also reflects the tensions that could exist between Métis people and the indigenous peoples with whom they traded and lived, as well as between Métis people and European settlers.

This is a story from the oral tradition of the Secwépemc people. It is a story about the creation of the lake Shuswap. According to this story, the lake was created when two men from Egulac (a place located near present-day Kamloops, British Columbia) made a noise like the noise of a falling tree. The two men were identified as Ptah and Tahmisko. They were out hunting one evening when they heard a noise like the noise of a falling tree. They went to investigate and saw that it was coming from the lake. They approached the lake and saw that the water was calm and still. Ptah and Tahmisko were both thirsty, so they leaned down and drank from the lake. As they drank, they made a noise like the noise of a falling tree. When they finished drinking, they stood up and made that noise again. And again, and again. Eventually, they left the lake and went back to Egulac. But the noise they made at the lake stayed with the lake. And that is how the lake got its name.

There is a variation of this story that involves three men from Egulac. One of the men made the noise at the lake, but the other two men told him to be quiet. One of the men went to the lake and made the noise again, and again, and again. But the two other men told him to stop making that noise. Eventually, the man who made the noise at the lake went back to Egulac, but the noise stayed with the lake.

But Raven and Owl had other plans. They did not want to ruin the dance. They wanted to join in the dance. So they snuck into the village and hid. When the dance began, they crept out of their hiding places and joined in the dance.

The people of the village were startled at first. They had never seen wolves dance before. But soon the people joined in the dance. The two wolves led the dance. They showed the people new steps. The people learned to dance like wolves.

After the dance was over, the people of the village fed Owl and Raven. They were happy to have the wolves as their friends. From then on, the people of the village welcomed the two shape-shifters. And the two wolves were happy to have a place to dance.

Owl and Frog were surprised. "We have come in peace," they said. "We have not come to fight. We have come to share in the feast."

But the people of Barkerville were not convinced. "You have taken our gold. You have ruined our lives."

In the story "The Two-Headed Serpent," from the Mouni Ki Wajpa, an oral tradition of the Ktunaxa people, these two beings are the helpers of the Creator. They come to the village to warn the people of a two-headed serpent that is approaching. The people do not recognize them, and some even try to kill them. But Owl and Frog manage to escape and make it to the mountain, where they are fed and clothed by the Creator. The Creator then sends them back to the village, this time with a message: the two-headed serpent is a symbol of war. If the people continue to fight among themselves, the serpent will keep coming. But if they live in peace, the serpent will go away.

This story is one of several tales in the Ktunaxa people's oral tradition that warn of the consequences of war. In these stories, the Ktunaxa people were warned of the coming of Europeans, who brought war and disease.

Ishkote and Taka had been brothers in the spirit world, too. They had come to the village together, but they were not to eat or drink together. Ishkote had found a good spring, but Taka did not want his water. Instead, Taka went off to the forest to find his own water.

Ishkote and Taka were not really brothers. They were two parts of one being. Ishkote was the thinking part. He was the one who planned and thought about the future. Taka was the feeling part. He was the one who loved and was loved. Ishkote and Taka were Raven and Crow. They were always together, but they were never the same.

The story is often told as a parable illustrating the concept of paying it forward, i.e. doing a good deed now in the hope that it will be reciprocated later. In this story, the two men from Egulac are said to represent the first two people who ever learned this lesson. They had learned it from their parents, who had learned it from their parents, and so on, back to the first couple who had settled the land. The story is often told to illustrate the concept of paying it forward, but it also illustrates the concept of reciprocity, which is a two-way street. In order for paying it forward to work, both parties must be willing to participate.

Variants
There are several variants of this story, some of which have nothing to do with the concept of paying it forward. One variant is told in some Native American communities to illustrate the concept of the circle of life. In this version, the two men are told to continue walking even though they are tired, until they come to the place where they started. Only then will they have walked a complete circle and will have truly learned the lesson of the story.

The explosion caused a vacuum, and this vacuum caused the water in the lake to be sucked in between Egulac and Shuswap. Once the two men had quenched their thirst, they went away from the lake. The story of the Egulac is often used to explain the origin of winter, but it also has deeper symbolic meaning. This is a version of the origin story of Ktunaxa, a Dene/Athapaskan tribe of southeastern British Columbia, Canada. The story is told by Thomas "Big Bear" Harris, a Ktunaxa from the Egulac band. In the story, the two men represent the first two Ktunaxa hunters who came down from the mountains and settled near the lake that would later be called Ktunaxa. The mountain is said to represent the old world of the Ktunaxa, their traditional territory stretching from the Rocky Mountains to the Purcells. The lake is said to represent the new world, the world of the Ktunaxa as it is today. According to Harris, the story shows that the Ktunaxa have always known that the world as it is today will one day end.

This is the story of the Egulac, a group of hunters who were always on the move in the wintertime, according to a legend told by the Ktunaxa people of the Columbia Plateau in present-day British Columbia. The story is often told as a cautionary tale, to show the dangers of not sharing resources with others.

Variants
There are several variants of this story, involving different tribes and different animals. In one version, told by the Cree, it is two brothers who are hunting caribou. In another, told by the Blackfoot, it is two young men who are out hunting and come across a woman who is pregnant. In yet another, told by the Shuswap, it is two friends who are out berry-picking.

In each version, the moral is the same: "If you are kind and share, you will be fed. If you are mean and keep to yourself, you will starve."

The people of Shalimar, moved by their sincere apologies, welcome them back into the village and share their food with them.

This story, like many other stories from around the world, uses the trickster figure to explore themes of hospitality, generosity, and forgiveness.
